summary.text: For \(k=31\) and \(s=1\), the distinct integers \(5\) and \(1829=31\cdot59\) give the same sum: \(1/32+1/36=1/32+1/62+1/90+1/1860=17/288\). Thus their fractional parts coincide, contradicting pairwise distinctness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(n;k,s)=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{1}{(d+k)^s}.
\]
The conjecture claims, in particular, that for every pair of positive integers \(k,s\), the fractional parts of the numbers \(S(n;k,s)\), as \(n\) ranges over the positive integers, are pairwise distinct.

We disprove this by taking
\[
k=31,\qquad s=1,
\]
and comparing the two distinct positive integers
\[
n_1=5,\qquad n_2=1829.
\]

First consider \(n_1=5\). Since \(5\) is prime, its positive divisors are exactly \(1\) and \(5\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(5;31,1)
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{5+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}\\
 &=\frac{36+32}{32\cdot36}\\
 &=\frac{68}{1152}
 =\frac{17}{288}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now factor the second integer:
\[
1829=31\cdot59.
\]
Both factors are prime. Indeed, to check that \(31\) is prime it suffices to test the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{31}<6\), namely \(2,3,5\), none of which divides \(31\). Likewise, \(\sqrt{59}<8\), and none of \(2,3,5,7\) divides \(59\). The primes \(31\) and \(59\) are distinct, so the positive divisors of their product are exactly
\[
1,\ 31,\ 59,\ 31\cdot59=1829.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(1829;31,1)
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{31+31}
   +\frac1{59+31}+\frac1{1829+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}.
\end{aligned}
\]
A common denominator for these four fractions is
\[
44640=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot31.
\]
With this denominator, the four numerators are respectively
\[
\frac{44640}{32}=1395,
\qquad
\frac{44640}{62}=720,
\qquad
\frac{44640}{90}=496,
\qquad
\frac{44640}{1860}=24.
\]
Their sum is
\[
1395+720+496+24=2635.
\]
Thus
\[
S(1829;31,1)=\frac{2635}{44640}.
\]
Since \(44640=288\cdot155\) and \(2635=17\cdot155\), this reduces to
\[
S(1829;31,1)=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
We have therefore obtained the exact equality
\[
S(5;31,1)=S(1829;31,1)=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
In particular, these two rational numbers have the same fractional part. More explicitly, \(0<17/288<1\), so each fractional part is itself equal to \(17/288\).

But \(5\) and \(1829\) are distinct positive integers, while \(k=31\) and \(s=1\) are both positive. Hence this equality directly contradicts the conjectured pairwise distinctness of the fractional parts for every positive \(k,s\). Therefore the conjecture is false.
